source_title: Guy Stern A Future to Build

paragraphs.text: In November 1937, fifteen-year-old Guy Stern boarded a ship for America. His parents, brother and sister remained in Germany. He hoped that they would follow him.

The Nazis were making life more dangerous for Jewish families. Friends stopped speaking to Guy, and his sports club removed him because he was Jewish. His parents arranged for him to live with an aunt and uncle in St. Louis.

Before he left, his father found an English teacher for him. There was a new language to learn and a new country to understand. At fifteen, Guy needed skills that could help him begin again. He also had a goal: once he reached America, he would try to bring his family to safety.

Five days after arriving in St. Louis, Guy was attending an American high school. His teachers welcomed him. He joined the swimming team and worked on the school newspaper. Taking part in school life helped him find his place.

Money was a problem. A teacher helped him find work in the school lunchroom, and later he worked in hotels. He studied while earning money. He also searched for someone who could help bring his family to America.
These were difficult responsibilities for a teenager. Yet he was discovering new interests and making plans. Writing for the newspaper gave him another goal: he wanted to become a journalist.

Later, he found work at a hotel across the street from his university. Sometimes he hurried into class still wearing his work uniform. His wish to study was shaping practical decisions about his life.

When the United States entered the war, Guy wanted to serve. He applied for work in Navy intelligence, where language skills were useful. His application was refused because he had not been born in America.

In 1943, he was drafted into the U.S. Army. At Camp Ritchie, he learned to question German prisoners and understand military information. The language of the country he had escaped now gave him an important way to help.

In June 1944, Guy landed in Normandy, France, three days after D-Day. He returned to Europe wearing an American uniform. His questions could provide information for other soldiers. The teenager who once needed help leaving Germany now had skills that his new country needed.
During the fighting in France, Guy found a familiar name among the German prisoners. It belonged to someone he knew from his old sports club.
Years earlier, that club had told Guy's family that Jewish children could no longer belong. Now one of its former members was a prisoner, and Guy was the American soldier asking the questions.
According to Guy's account, he questioned the man at night, with a light shining on the prisoner. Guy kept his own identity hidden. He did not tell the man who he was.
The boy pushed out of a sports club had grown into a trained soldier. His knowledge of German life had become useful in the fight against the Nazis.
After the war, Guy learned that his parents, brother and sister had been murdered in the Holocaust. His efforts to rescue them had failed. This loss would remain part of his life.
He still hoped to become a journalist. With a letter of recommendation from an army officer, he went to the New York Times. However, the newspaper had no job for him.
Guy returned several times, but the situation did not change. Eventually, he chose another direction. He worked as a waiter and went back to university.
His goal changed as he learned more. He studied literature and later became a professor. A plan that had failed led him towards work he would continue for many years.

At fifteen, Guy could not know what his future would hold. He had years ahead of him in which to learn, discover abilities and change direction. The decisions he made at school became part of the adult he would become.
He needed help from relatives, teachers and others. Some goals remained out of reach, and some losses could never be repaired. Still, he kept making room for new possibilities.

For young people, his life offers an important message: set goals, accept help and keep learning. You can change your plans as you grow. Believing that life can become better can give you a reason to take the next step.
Guy once entered an American classroom as a refugee. Later, he spent decades teaching students. Their success became one of the greatest rewards of his life.
